title: Stool Examination & Concentration Techniques (Parasitology)

references.label: WHO Laboratory Quality Management System Handbook

purpose: To detect intestinal parasites (protozoa, helminth eggs/larvae) in stool by combining direct examination with a concentration technique that increases the density of parasitic elements relative to fecal debris, improving detection sensitivity for light infections.
principle: Direct wet-mount examination of stool can miss light infections because parasitic elements are diluted among a large volume of fecal debris; concentration techniques exploit density differences (flotation, where parasitic elements float in a high-density solution while debris sinks, or sedimentation, where parasitic elements settle through a lower-density medium while lighter debris is decanted away) to increase the proportion of parasitic elements in the material actually examined under the microscope.
requiredMaterials: Concentration technique supplies (per the specific flotation or sedimentation method in use)
requiredReagents: Saline and iodine (for direct wet mount)
Concentration solution appropriate to the method (flotation or sedimentation) in use

procedure.instruction: Perform a direct wet-mount examination of a small stool portion in both saline (for motility of trophozoites and general morphology) and iodine (which stains internal structures of cysts/eggs, aiding identification) as an initial screen.

procedure.note: Flotation and sedimentation techniques differ in their principle, target solute density, and which parasitic elements they concentrate best — follow the specific validated method in use rather than assuming a single universal protocol.
procedure.instruction: Prepare a concentrated specimen using the laboratory's chosen flotation or sedimentation technique, following that method's specific solution, timing, and processing steps.
Examine the concentrated preparation systematically under low then high power, scanning the entire coverslip area methodically to avoid missing sparse elements.
Identify any parasitic elements observed by morphology (size, shape, internal structures) and record the developmental stage seen (e.g. trophozoite, cyst, egg, larva).
Report findings using the laboratory's standard terminology, correlating direct and concentrated examination findings.

observations: Record parasitic elements observed, their developmental stage, approximate quantity, and which examination (direct vs. concentrated) detected them.
interpretation: A negative result on a single stool specimen does not exclude parasitic infection, since some organisms are shed intermittently — multiple specimens over different days are often recommended per the ordering clinician's protocol, a decision outside the laboratory's scope.
precautions: Examine fresh (or appropriately preserved) specimens — some parasitic forms degrade quickly in unpreserved stool at room temperature.
Use correct technique for each concentration method, since technique errors directly reduce detection sensitivity.
limitations: No single concentration technique is optimal for every parasite type; sensitivity varies by organism, technique, and specimen freshness/preservation.
Compact, foundational coverage only — this entry does not enumerate organism-specific identification keys.
biosafetyNotes: Stool specimens are biohazardous and may contain infectious parasitic stages; use standard precautions, appropriate PPE, and dispose of specimens/waste per biohazard protocol.
